implementation_notes: There is no Java-level prefetch intrinsic. The JVM's memory model (the same release/acquire framework as C++11) has no prefetch opcode in the managed surface, and the JIT inserts its own prefetches for array and field accesses it can prove are hot. So the practical levers are: layout (primitive arrays and struct-of-arrays beat object graphs for hot numeric work - this is the data-locality pattern in its JVM form), avoiding the extra copy that a boxed Integer or a wrapper adds, and for files, letting the OS readahead work by reading sequentially through a large buffer. JDK's Panama/FFM API exposes raw memory, and one can reach a prefetch via a native call, but this is not a normal Java move. Measure with async-profiler or JFR before adding anything: on a managed runtime the fix is almost always the layout, not a hint.
idiom_name: no managed prefetch; use array-of-primitives layout and OS readahead (the JVM/JIT's own prefetching handles what it can prove)
pitfalls: There is no managed prefetch intrinsic; reaching one via a native call via Panama/FFM is an unusual, unmaintainable move.
Double[] versus double[] is the JVM's real prefetch decision: a boxed array is a pointer chase and a dereference per element.
The JIT inserts its own prefetches for provably-hot accesses, so a manual hint is redundant at best.
For files, the win is sequential large reads (OS readahead), not a cache hint - read with a large buffer, not byte-at-a-time.
